did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a list of Jacob’s sons, called here “the sons of Israel,” and names the twelve sons in this order: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.

The sons of Judah mentioned at the beginning of the list are Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er, Judah’s firstborn, is described as wicked in the LORD’s sight—and according to the text, the LORD put him to death.
Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, bore him Perez and Zerah. Thus, the text concludes that the sons of Judah mentioned here number five: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah.
Carmi was the father of Achar, also called “the troubler of Israel,” because he violated the ban. In this way, the chapter connects Achar with the act of violating what had been placed under the ban.
The line from Perez continues through Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse. Nahshon is described as a leader of the people of Judah.
Jesse is listed as the son of Obed and the father of David. In the list of Jesse’s sons, David appears seventh, after Eliab, Abinadab, Shimea, Nethanel, Raddai, and Ozem.
Jesse had two sisters who are mentioned by name: Zeruiah and Abigail. Zeruiah’s sons were Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, and Abigail gave birth to Amasa.
The chapter presents a genealogy that extends to Bezalel: Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezalel.

Jair, a descendant of Hezron through the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead, is described as possessing twenty-three towns in the land of Gilead. Later, sixty towns associated with the family of Machir are also mentioned.
Sheshan had no sons, only daughters. He gave his daughter to Jarha, his Egyptian servant, and the line descended from them continues in the following verses down to Elishama.
